Name: Instructions of Shuruppak
Short Description: A Sumerian wisdom composition framed as fatherly advice from the legendary king Shuruppak to his son Ziusudra. Its maxims address speech, property, household management, social conduct, and personal restraint. Copied for centuries within the scribal curriculum, the work likely helped shape the ethical and administrative habits expected of educated officials, although its precise institutional setting varied over time.

Name: Administrative Tablets from Ebla
Short Description: A royal-palace archive of roughly 17,000 tablets and fragments from Ebla. Written mainly in Eblaite and Sumerian cuneiform, the documents record diplomacy, trade, tribute, taxation, personnel, landholding, ritual offerings, and scribal education. Together they reveal how economic administration, court politics, and temple ritual were integrated within a powerful third-millennium Syrian state.

Their highly formulaic accounting language preserves the routine machinery through which the Lagash polity organized production, redistribution, cult, and dependent labor.

Name: Royal Inscriptions of Sargon of Akkad
Short Description: Royal inscriptions issued in the name of Sargon of Akkad commemorate conquests, offerings, building activity, and the expansion of Akkadian power. The texts present military success as evidence of divine election and helped establish a language through which later rulers could frame territorial rule as sacred and historically exemplary.

Name: The Exaltation of Inanna
Short Description: A Sumerian hymn traditionally attributed to Enheduanna. Speaking in the first person, the narrator describes expulsion from office, appeals to the moon god Nanna, and invokes Inanna’s overwhelming power for restoration. The poem transforms personal and political crisis into a cosmic drama of divine justice, making religious praise simultaneously an act of self-vindication and a powerful statement about sacred authority.

Name: Eridu Genesis
Short Description: A fragmentary Sumerian composition preserved principally on an Old Babylonian tablet from Nippur. It recounts the establishment of cities and kingship before a divinely sent flood, from which the pious king Ziusudra survives in a boat and receives exceptional divine favor. Although the surviving text is second-millennium BCE, it draws on older traditions and presents kingship as a sacred trust vulnerable to periodic divine judgment and renewal.

Name: Code of Ur-Nammu
Short Description: The earliest substantially preserved Mesopotamian law collection, attributed to Ur-Nammu or possibly completed under his successor Shulgi. Its prologue grounds royal justice in divine order and presents the king as protector of the vulnerable. The surviving provisions often prescribe monetary compensation and can be read as part of a wider effort to stabilize property, labor, and social relations after political upheaval, though they did not constitute a modern comprehensive code.

Name: Gilgamesh and Agga
Short Description: A Sumerian heroic poem about Uruk’s resistance to the authority of Agga of Kish. Gilgamesh first consults the city’s elders, who advise submission, and then its able-bodied men, who support resistance. His choice of the latter dramatizes tension between caution and martial resolve; after defeating Agga, however, Gilgamesh releases him. The poem can therefore be read as affirming Uruk’s independence and warrior loyalty while also presenting mercy and political restraint as components of kingship.

Short Description: An Akkadian dialogue in which a master repeatedly proposes an action and his servant supplies persuasive reasons both to perform it and to avoid it.
